action.apply-tooltip-clean: Everything on screen is already applied.
action.apply-tooltip-pending: Send the changes on screen to the background service.
action.apply-tooltip-service-stopped: The rules on screen are not applied to the service. It is stopped, so Apply saves them to your rules file for now and stays available until the service can take them.

service.title: Service management
service.description: NetRuleRouter runs as a background service. Installing, removing, starting and stopping it needs administrator rights — the system asks for them.
service.admin-hint: These actions require administrator approval — asked once per session.

status.transition-hint: This is normal and usually takes a few seconds — no action needed.

reason.not-registered: Service is not registered in the system.

action.stop-tooltip: Stops the background service. By default all routes are removed and every connection returns to your main connection; leak-protection blocks are removed. (Turn on "Keep rule routes on the additional adapter after pause/stop" in Settings to keep your routed sites on the additional adapter — e.g. a work/corporate adapter.) Note: simply closing the app keeps routing active, because the service keeps running.

start-mode.heading: When the service starts
start-mode.help: “Start with the system” keeps your rules enforced from boot, before anyone logs in (best for always-on or managed setups). “Start when the app opens” runs the service only while you use NetRuleRouter and lets the app start it without an administrator prompt every time. Changing this needs administrator approval.
start-mode.help-with-system-only: “Start with the system” keeps your rules enforced from boot, before anyone logs in. Changing this needs administrator approval.

launch-tray.label: Also start the tray at sign-in
launch-tray.description: The service starts at boot before anyone logs in and cannot open the tray itself. This starts the tray icon when you sign in — the same setting as “Start the tray automatically at sign-in” in General.

service.crash-recovery: After a failure the service restarts by itself; if failures repeat, the network returns to normal and the service keeps trying, less often.

admin-auto-revoke.title: Administrator rights
admin-auto-revoke.disable-label: Do not revoke administrator approval automatically
admin-auto-revoke.note: After you approve administrator access, it stays available without new prompts. If it sits unused for this long, the app gives it up on its own; the next administrative action will ask again.

recovery.description: If the service was killed without shutting down, its packet filters, DNS redirect and routes can stay behind and cut this machine off the network. This removes them.
recovery.tooltip: Needs administrator rights. Connections open right now may drop.

update.elsewhere: The system starts the background service from another folder, not the one this application runs from.
update.older: The running background service is an older build than this application.
update.tooltip: Needs administrator rights. The service restarts, so routing pauses for a moment. Your rules and settings are kept.

stale-process.description: The service program file was updated, but the service is still running the previous version. Restart it to run the update.
stale-process.tooltip: Needs administrator rights. Routing pauses for a moment while the service restarts.

offer-install.label: Offer to install the service when it is missing
offer-install.description: Without the background service the app applies no rules at all, so it offers to install one. Dismissing the offer holds it back for a week; turning this off stops it entirely.

console.title: Command-line console
console.description: NetRuleRouter ships a small console for service tasks: install, start, stop and check the service. Add its folder to your PATH to run it as "nrr-cli" from any terminal.
console.path-registered: The console can be run from any terminal.
console.path-not-registered: The console can only be run from its own folder — and in PowerShell you still have to spell it ".\nrr-cli.exe", because a bare name is not searched for in the current directory.
console.path-reachable-not-ours: The folder is already on your PATH, but the entry was not added by NetRuleRouter — so there is nothing here to add or take away.
console.add-to-path-tooltip: Adds the console's folder to your personal PATH. It affects your account only, needs no administrator rights, and changes nothing else on the list.
console.remove-from-path-tooltip: Removes the entry NetRuleRouter added to your personal PATH. Nothing else on the list is touched, and terminals that are already open keep the PATH they started with.
console.path-added: The console was added to your PATH.
console.path-already-present: The console was already on your PATH.
console.path-failed: Could not add the console to your PATH.
console.path-removed: The console was removed from your PATH.
console.path-was-not-present: Nothing to remove — this entry was not put there by NetRuleRouter.
console.path-remove-failed: Could not remove the console from your PATH.
console.new-terminal-hint: Terminals that are already open keep the PATH they started with. Open a new one, or run this line in the current one:

presets.title: Presets and settings
presets.description: Import or export rules in plain-text format. Each route has its own preset file; the other route's rules are carried over from the active revision on import.
presets.full-settings-description: Export adapter bindings, your rules for both routes (those for other operating systems included), the paths of your rules files, the default route and leak protection as a single YAML file. Useful for backing up or transferring your settings.

bundled-presets.title: Bundled presets
bundled-presets.label: Show the bundled-preset quick-load row in Rules
bundled-presets.description: Shows a quick-load dropdown of bundled country/demo presets above the rules table. The "Hide" button on that row also turns this off.

user-folder.title: My rule sets
user-folder.description: Point the quick-load dropdown at your own folder instead of the sets that come with the app. The folder can hold "rules_primary.txt" and "rules_secondary.txt" directly, or one subfolder per set — each subfolder's name becomes the entry in the dropdown.
user-folder.placeholder: Using the rule sets that come with the app
user-folder.dialog-title: Choose the folder with your rule sets
user-folder.use-bundled-path: Point at the sets that come with the app

save-as-set.button: Save current rules as a set...
save-as-set.needs-folder: Choose a folder above first — that is where a new set is saved.
save-as-set.title: Save rules as a set
save-as-set.prompt: The current rules of both routes are saved as a new set in your folder. Name it so you can tell it apart later, for example "work" or "home".
save-as-set.name-invalid: A name cannot contain \ / : or ".." — it is a folder name, not a path.
save-as-set.folder-missing: Choose a folder for the set.

bundled-write-warning.title: This folder belongs to the app
bundled-write-warning.body: You are saving into the folder the app keeps its own rule sets in. Updating the app replaces that folder, and your set is lost with it. Pick a folder of your own above to keep sets safely.
bundled-write-warning.dont-ask: I understand — do not ask again

note.logs-diagnostics: Preview controls are available on dedicated screens.
note.experimental: Early features that are still being tested. They are off by default and may change or be removed.
note.route-labels: You can rename the two routes for the UI without changing routing behavior.
note.presets: When enabled, selecting a preset for one route automatically opens a file picker for the other route.

allow-mode-a.label: Allow the legacy routing method (watching system DNS)
allow-mode-a.note: Watching system DNS is the legacy routing method, kept for reference only. It is not maintained, may not work, and may be removed in a future release; the supported method is the local DNS resolver. Turn this on only if you specifically need to choose it in the routing settings.

vm-section.label: Virtual machines screen
vm-section.note: Adds a Virtual machines screen under Rules that sends a hypervisor's traffic over the route you pick. Not verified on real hardware yet: the screen may be incomplete and the route may not apply to every machine.

detailed-mode.label: Detailed mode
detailed-mode.note: Shows extra fine-tuning switches under Settings → Routing. Off by default: without it, NetRuleRouter uses sensible defaults for them. The main routing switches stay visible either way.

field.notify-suggestion-changes: Tell me when the suggested-addresses list changes
field.notify-block-notices: Tell me when a connection gets blocked
field.hide-block-notice-addresses-tooltip: Replaces the destination with a generic label instead of the real hostname — useful when your screen is being shared or recorded.
field.auto-confirm-adapter-id: Auto-confirm a reinstalled additional adapter when its name matches
field.auto-confirm-adapter-id-tooltip: When an additional adapter is reinstalled and gets a new ID, re-bind it automatically if the saved name uniquely matches a live adapter. Turn off to confirm each change manually via the banner.
field.block-secondary-traffic: Block connections when the additional route is unavailable
field.rules-file-change-mode: When rules file changes on disk
field.tray-notice-opacity-note: Applies to notifications shown from the tray. Restart the tray for it to take effect.
field.notify-rule-duplicates: Tell me when a rule is set on both routes

vpn-gateways.title: Other VPNs you allowed
vpn-gateways.note: Their servers can be reached over the main connection while leak protection is on, for the VPN's own connection only.
vpn-gateways.removed-status: The VPN server {address} is no longer let through.

zone-ip-priority.label: Zone vs. IP priority
zone-ip-priority.description: When a Zone rule and an Exact IP rule both match the same destination, choose which takes priority.

failure-policy.title: Apply failure policy
failure-policy.description: Choose how the service handles partial failures during multi-step rule application.

best-effort.label: Best effort (recommended)
best-effort.description: Rules that can't be enforced on this host (app not installed, host not yet resolved, missing adapter) are skipped and reported; the rest are applied. Default.

all-or-nothing.label: All or nothing
all-or-nothing.description: If any single rule can't be enforced, the whole apply rolls back. Exact-or-nothing.

pre-flight.label: Check first, then all or nothing
pre-flight.description: Checks the change before touching anything, and refuses to start when it cannot be applied as one piece — a very large rule set is applied in several parts, and this option would rather stop than leave half of it live. Rules that would be stored without enforcing anything (a program that is not installed) are reported, not blocked.

failure-policy.requires-elevation: Changing this setting requires administrator elevation.

pause.title: Apply rules
pause.persistence-hint: Disabling stops applying rules for the time chosen under “Turn rules back on”: they come back on their own when it is up, and with “When I turn them back on” only when you do.
pause.no-tray-warning: Tray is not running. Rules apply only while the tray is active.

default-route.title: Default route
default-route.description: Where traffic that matches no rule goes. Rules always take priority.

leak-protection.note-off: If the additional connection drops, traffic continues over your main connection.
leak-protection.note-sites: What your rules send through the additional connection never goes out the main one while strict blocking of shared addresses is on, as it is by default. Everything else keeps working, except sites that share an address with a routed one.
leak-protection.note-everything: Nothing leaves except through the additional connection, your local network and what your rules send over the main connection. If the additional connection drops, the internet waits until it returns.

routing-method.title: Routing method
routing-method.scope-note: The settings in this group apply to every user of this computer and need administrator approval to change, except the shared-address ones, which are yours alone.

enforcement-mode.label: How routed traffic is enforced
enforcement-mode.note: The resolver answers site-name lookups itself and sets up the route before the answer reaches the program, so even the first connection takes the right route. It takes over system DNS while the service runs. Changes apply immediately — no service restart needed.

dns-via-secondary.label: DNS through the tunnel
dns-via-secondary.note: Site names are looked up through the additional connection instead of your provider's resolver, so the provider can neither see nor alter the answers. Some providers return a wrong or empty address for certain sites, which makes those sites fail to load even when routing is correct. If the additional connection is not available, lookups fall back to the main one. Off by default.

dns-fast-answers.label: Fast DNS answers
dns-fast-answers.note: Answer apps immediately; route protection finishes in the background. Turning this off can slow down page loads.

fake-ip.label: Route sites over virtual addresses (fake-IP)
fake-ip.note: Each routed site is answered with its own virtual address, so routing stays per-site even when several sites share one real server address — and protection no longer races the first connection. Requires the local DNS resolver. On Windows, turning this on loads the bundled Wintun virtual-adapter driver (signed by WireGuard LLC). On by default on a new install.

fake-ip-udp-relay.label: Fake-IP UDP relay (experimental)
fake-ip-udp-relay.note: Carry QUIC/HTTP-3 through the relay instead of forcing browsers to fall back to TCP.

fake-ip-instant-rst.label: Instant reset when the additional route is unavailable
fake-ip-instant-rst.note: On (default): apps get an immediate connection reset when the additional route can't be resolved, so they can retry or fail over right away. Off: connections are held for up to 10 seconds while the route comes back, instead of resetting immediately.

hosts-bypass.label: Resolve routed domains bypassing the hosts file
hosts-bypass.note: On (default): routed domains are resolved directly against your DNS server, so a local hosts/adblock entry pinning a routed site to 127.0.0.1 cannot silently disable its routing. Turn off only if you rely on hosts-file overrides for the sites you route.

auto-rules.title: Auto-rules
auto-rules.label: Missing companion domains
auto-rules.note: A routed site often loads its images and video from other domains your rules do not list, so the page opens but its content does not. By default NetRuleRouter collects these missing domains and offers them in the tray — nothing is added to your rules without your confirmation. “Apply automatically” adds them for you; “Off” stops collecting them altogether.
auto-rules.auto-save-note: Added addresses are written straight into the rules files your routes are linked to.
auto-rules.eager-label: Offer content-delivery domains without waiting for analysis
auto-rules.eager-note: Off by default. Content-delivery domains are usually named alike, so this makes media load sooner. Advertising and tracking networks are named alike too, so some of what appears will not be worth routing — review before you accept it.

doh-lockdown.title: Block browser DoH/DoT
doh-lockdown.label: Block browser DoH/DoT
doh-lockdown.note: Browsers that resolve names over DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) or DNS-over-TLS (DoT) hide their queries, so routed sites resolved that way bypass your rules and leak protection. Turning this on blocks known encrypted-DNS endpoints so name resolution falls back to plaintext DNS that NetRuleRouter can observe.
doh-lockdown.scope-leak-protection-only: Only while leak protection is active (recommended)
doh-lockdown.scope-leak-protection-only-note: Blocks encrypted DNS only while leak protection blocks all traffic, where DoH would otherwise defeat observation. Leaves DoH working the rest of the time. Recommended.
doh-lockdown.scope-always-note: Blocks encrypted DNS at all times, even when leak protection is off — maximum observability, but it breaks DoH/HTTP-3 for every app and can slow name resolution.
doh-lockdown.auto-note: Blocks encrypted DNS in browsers while your rules need to see site names, so the sites you route or block are seen and handled. Turn this off to set the blocking by hand.
doh-lockdown.auto-on: On: your rules route or block sites by name.
doh-lockdown.auto-off: Off: none of your rules needs site names.
doh-lockdown.details: Blocking works by denying connections to a known list of DoH/DoT resolver endpoints (edited below). Apps then fall back to the operating system's plaintext DNS, which the observer reads to keep routing and leak protection accurate. Some apps pin their own resolver and may show connection errors until DoH is turned off in their own settings; this does not affect apps that use the system resolver.

resolvers.requires-admin: This is a shared, machine-wide list. Saving changes requires administrator approval.
resolvers.description: Endpoints blocked when the lockdown is active. Add a public resolver by IP address or hostname; untick a row to keep it in the list but stop blocking it.
resolvers.save-failed: Could not save the resolver list:
resolvers.load-failed: Could not load the resolver list:
resolvers.not-read: The resolver list could not be read, so it cannot be changed now.
resolvers.uac-declined: Administrator approval was declined; the resolver list was not saved.

hosts-file.label: OS hosts file
hosts-file.note: The OS hosts file can redirect or block a hostname before NetRuleRouter sees it (ad-block lists often map hosts to 127.0.0.1). NetRuleRouter never edits it — open the folder to inspect or edit it yourself (requires administrator).

liveness-window.label: Additional tunnel liveness window
liveness-window.note: Optional. When set, NetRuleRouter actively pings the additional adapter's next hop; if it stays unreachable for this many seconds, the additional connection counts as down even though the adapter is still up and no traffic has failed yet: with leak protection on, what it carries is blocked; with it off, that traffic goes over the main connection. Off by default. It may false-positive if the tunnel peer silently drops ICMP (many VPNs do), so leave it off unless you know the peer answers pings.

rule-lock.heading: Who can change the rules

allow.label: Allow users to change routing rules
allow.tooltip: On (default): anyone signed in to this computer can add, edit and apply their own routing rules. Turn it off on company laptops so only an administrator changes the rules. Pausing routing and the route settings (connections, default route, leak protection) stay with each user.

rule-lock.help: Affects the whole machine and needs administrator approval. While it is off, the Rules view is read-only for everyone: viewing, searching and exporting still work, but adding, editing, applying, importing and resetting to the baseline are turned off. The background service refuses the change as well, so the lock does not depend on this window.

vpn-client.title: Your VPN client
vpn-client.note: Point NetRuleRouter at the program you use as your VPN so its traffic keeps flowing over your main link while leak protection is on.
vpn-client.external-address-auto: Check the external address each time the additional route connects
vpn-client.external-address-auto-note: Once per connection, asks a public address server through the additional route which address the internet sees, and shows it in a notice. Off by default: the request leaves through your VPN. The “Check external address” button works either way.

providers.note: Programs that keep working over your main link while leak protection is on, such as your VPN client. Type a program's full path to add one.
providers.need-path: Type the program's full path first.
providers.removed: {name} was removed. Leak protection no longer keeps it working over your main link.

vpn-gateway.title: Other VPNs (corporate)
vpn-gateway.note: For a VPN that connects only from one network, such as a work VPN allowed only from abroad: its gateway gets a rule for the channel you choose, so it always connects through that channel. If that channel is down, the VPN does not connect over the other one.
vpn-gateway.observer-off: On this system NetRuleRouter cannot see where a program connects. Type the gateway address below.
vpn-gateway.empty: {program} has not connected anywhere on the internet recently. Start the VPN and let it try to connect, then search again.
vpn-gateway.manual-placeholder: Or type the gateway address or name
vpn-gateway.manual-invalid: This is neither an address nor a host name.
vpn-gateway.apply-hint: The rules are in your list now. Apply the changes to put them into effect.

shared-addresses.title: Shared addresses (one IP serving several sites)
shared-addresses.routing-axis: While the additional adapter is up: whether a shared IP is routed through it.
shared-addresses.blocking-axis: While the additional adapter is down: whether shared addresses are blocked.

kill-switch.title: Leak protection
kill-switch.description: Leak protection decides what happens to your traffic while the additional connection is unavailable: the VPN is disconnected, not started yet, or was reinstalled under a new name. "Routed sites" holds what your rules send through the additional connection — sites, IPs and applications; everything else keeps working as usual. "Everything" holds all traffic except your local network and what your rules send over the main connection.
kill-switch.coverage-note: How coverage works: protection tracks the IP addresses a routed site resolves to, learned by watching your system's DNS. It extends automatically as new addresses appear (e.g. when a site behind a CDN rotates IPs), but a brand-new address has a brief unprotected moment until it is seen. Apps that resolve names themselves over DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) bypass this — turn off DoH in the browser/app for full protection. A diagnostic ping is the hardest case: it fires a single packet the instant a name resolves — before protection can catch up — and pinging a bare IP address skips name-based routing entirely; neither reflects how apps normally connect.
kill-switch.allow-dns-label: While everything is held, look up site names over the main connection
kill-switch.allow-dns-note: On by default, so site names keep resolving while the additional connection is down — only through the DNS servers of your main connection and only on the DNS port. The cost: those servers, usually your provider's, see the names of the sites you open, including the ones your rules send through the additional connection; the traffic itself stays held. Turn it off for strict blocking: with name lookups cut too, nothing works until the additional connection returns.
kill-switch.shared-strict-label: Strict: also block addresses shared with regular sites (may break them)
kill-switch.shared-strict-note: On (the default): safer. No traffic of routed sites goes out through the main connection, but some ordinary sites that share an address with them may stop opening until the additional adapter is back. Off: more convenient. Ordinary sites keep opening while the additional adapter is down, but some traffic of routed sites may go out through the main connection.
kill-switch.shared-smart-warning: Leak protection strictness is reduced: shared addresses excluded from blocking —
kill-switch.shared-smart-list-unavailable: The running service reports how many addresses were excluded, but not which ones.
kill-switch.block-all-active-banner: Leak protection is holding all traffic: the additional connection can't be found (down, not started, or reinstalled under a new ID). The internet waits until it returns; reconnect the VPN or assign the adapter again.
kill-switch.block-all-warn-label: Warn while leak protection is holding all traffic
kill-switch.block-all-warn-note: On by default: a banner appears while the additional connection is down and everything waits for it. Turn it off if you deliberately keep the service running with the VPN disconnected (e.g. from OS startup) and don't want the reminder.

protocols.label: Protocols leak protection cuts
protocols.desc: Which IP protocols leak protection drops. ICMP covers ping/traceroute. TCP/UDP are enforced at the connection layer; ICMP/IGMP/GRE/ESP at the packet layer. All on by default — uncheck to let a protocol through even while the block is active. ICMP, IGMP, GRE and ESP are cut for the whole computer, not only for your account.
protocols.tcp-tooltip: Most web, email and app traffic (HTTP/HTTPS and similar).
protocols.udp-tooltip: DNS, video calls, games and other real-time traffic.
protocols.icmp-tooltip: Ping and traceroute. These live only at the packet layer, so ICMP must be checked for the block to stop a ping.
protocols.igmp-tooltip: Multicast group membership on the local network.
protocols.gre-tooltip: A tunnelling protocol used by some VPNs (e.g. PPTP).
protocols.last-one-hint: To turn leak protection off, choose Off above.

local-networks.title: Local networks
local-networks.description: These networks stay reachable whatever your rules and leak protection do: a router, a printer or a virtual machine on them keeps working, and traffic to them goes straight there, never through the additional connection.
local-networks.empty: No local networks found yet. Add one below if you reach a virtual machine at an address this list does not show.

reason.too-wide: too wide to be a local network, stays blocked
reason.contains-rule-address: holds an address your rules name, stays blocked

local-networks.undecided-hint: A tick alone is what this computer does by default, not your answer. Confirm and the offer stops coming back.
local-networks.reject-not-private: {cidr} is not a local network — only private ranges can be kept reachable.
local-networks.reject-malformed: {cidr} is not a network address. Write it as 10.0.2.0/24.
local-networks.auto-accept: Keep newly found local networks reachable without asking
local-networks.auto-accept-hint: A hypervisor, WSL or a second VPN adds a network of its own over time. With this on they stay reachable and no question is shown; every network is still listed below and any of them can be refused.

local-suffixes.title: Home and local network names
local-suffixes.description: Names under these suffixes belong to the network you are on (a printer, a router, a NAS) and are resolved by that network, never sent down a route. One list for every user of this computer; changing it needs an administrator.
local-suffixes.covers-rules: covers your rules for {hosts}; those names keep following their rules
local-suffixes.save-failed: Could not save the network name list:
local-suffixes.load-failed: Could not load the network name list:
local-suffixes.not-read: The network name list could not be read, so it cannot be changed now.
local-suffixes.uac-declined: Administrator approval was declined; the network name list was not saved.

short-names.title: Short names
short-names.description: Work computers are often opened by a short name such as wiki. A work VPN that announces its network domain is picked up automatically. If yours does not, name the domain here.
short-names.enable: Complete short names with this domain

primary-probe.auto: Check the main route for new suggestions automatically
primary-probe.description: One short connection attempt per address, from the main connection. It answers whether the address is reachable there — not whether the site works there.
primary-probe.repeat: Do not re-check the same address for, s

doh-lockdown.what: This switch keeps programs from using DNS servers of their own, so every name lookup goes through NetRuleRouter and your domain rules can see it.
doh-lockdown.when-safe: Turning it off is safe if this program does not open the sites your rules route: its lookups will then simply go past your domain rules. Leave it on if you rely on leak protection for everything.

leak-protection.what: With leak protection set to Everything, IPv6 goes out only through the additional connection: while that connection is down or carries no IPv6, IPv6 waits. With Routed sites, only the IPv6 addresses of your routed sites are held, and only while the additional connection carries no IPv6.
leak-protection.when-safe: Turning leak protection off opens IPv6 again, but it also stops blocking your routed traffic when the additional route goes down. That is safe only if nothing you route needs to stay hidden, for example on a network you trust.

forwarded-traffic.title: WSL, containers and virtual machines
forwarded-traffic.description: Programs in WSL, containers and virtual machines reach the internet through this computer, yet leak protection does not see them on its own. Choose what they get while the additional route is down.

as-computer.label: Same as this computer (recommended)
as-computer.note: Addresses your rules send through the additional route reach them only through it, as they do your programs; while that route is down those stay closed, and when this computer blocks everything, so is their traffic. Works while leak protection is on.

unprotected.label: Do not protect
unprotected.note: While the additional route is down, they reach everything over the main route, including addresses your rules send through the additional one.

forwarded-traffic.unanswered: Not chosen yet: they are protected like this computer.
forwarded-traffic.choice: When the additional route is down

level.label: Log detail level
level.description: Controls how much detail appears in the Logs screen and is written to the log store.
level.desc-info: Normal operation messages. Recommended for everyday use.
level.desc-warning: Warnings about recoverable conditions (stale cache, brief unavailability).
level.desc-debug: Detailed trace output — rule matching decisions and availability snapshots.
level.desc-critical: Critical errors only. Minimum log volume.

browser-stub.label: Browser stub on connection block
browser-stub.description: When leak protection blocks a browser connection, show a built-in stub page instead of a silent connection error. Requires the process to be identified as a known browser.
browser-stub.experimental-warning: Experimental — behaviour may change without notice.

routing-behavior.ip-routing-note: Routing works by IP address. A website that checks and shows your IP (like 2ip.ru or whatismyipaddress.com) can still display your provider's address: its measurement endpoint often lives on a different IP than the page itself, or a single IP is shared by several sites. If you use a general-purpose VPN as the additional adapter, such a site can also keep showing your provider's IP and country when it is not one of your routed rules — that traffic goes over your primary link, while your routed sites still go through the VPN. This is a known limitation, not a routing failure. Per-site (per-hostname) steering on a shared IP is not supported yet.

include-subdomains.label: Also cover subdomains for domain rules (treat “example.com” as “example.com” + “*.example.com”)
include-subdomains.note: On by default: a rule for a site also covers that site's subdomains, so images and scripts from “cdn.example.com” take the same route as “example.com”. Applies to all your domain rules at once. It only catches subdomains of the SAME site — an IP-check served from a different provider (a third-party domain) still won't be covered — and it sends more traffic through the additional adapter. Turn it off to match the exact domain only.

app-rules-take-all.label: Programs in your rules take all their traffic
app-rules-take-all.description: A program you named in a rule sends everything it connects to over that rule's route, even to sites another rule sends the other way. Routing works per address, so those sites then go that route for every program on this computer.

shared-ip.label: When a routed domain shares an IP address with other sites
shared-ip.option-majority-of-ip: Route the shared IP only if most sites on it are yours (balanced)
shared-ip.option-majority-of-rules: Route the shared IP only if it holds most of your rules (cautious)
shared-ip.option-any-rule-domain: Always route the whole shared IP (aggressive)
shared-ip.note: Some sites (e.g. behind Cloudflare) share one IP with unrelated sites, and IP routing can't tell them apart. “Balanced” routes such an IP through the additional adapter only when your sites are the majority on it; “Cautious” only when that IP carries most of your rules; “Aggressive” always routes it (the others on it come along too). Truly separating two sites on one IP by name is not implemented in the current version.

prefer-primary.label: Main connection — selected sites through the additional one
prefer-primary.description: Only the sites, IPs and apps in your rules use the additional connection; all other traffic stays on your main connection. It routes by IP address, so sites on shared CDNs or apps using DNS-over-HTTPS can occasionally slip onto your main connection. What happens while the additional connection is down is up to leak protection.

prefer-secondary-when-available.label: Additional connection — exceptions through the main one
prefer-secondary-when-available.description: All traffic goes through the additional connection; only the exceptions in your rules use the main one. What happens while the additional connection is down is up to leak protection.

routing-behavior.default-mode-note: When no additional adapter is configured, your main connection is used by default.

retention.title: Revisions retention
retention.description: Controls how long superseded, rejected, and rolled-back revisions are kept before pruning.
retention.pin-lkg-hint: The most recent superseded revision is pinned and excluded from age and count limits.
retention.superseded-days-tooltip: Earlier versions of your rules that you can roll back to. Keep them longer for a longer history, or shorter to save disk space.
retention.superseded-count-tooltip: The most earlier versions kept, whatever their age. Once there are more, the oldest go first.
retention.rejected-days-tooltip: Rule sets the service refused to apply are kept this long, so the history still shows why they were refused.
retention.rolledback-days-tooltip: Rule sets that were undone, by you or after a failed apply, are kept this long so you can return to them.
retention.rolledback-count-tooltip: The most undone rule sets kept, whatever their age. Once there are more, the oldest go first.

autosave.label: Save changes automatically after
autosave.help: Changes on this page are saved automatically once you stop editing, when you press Apply, and when you leave the page. Reset restores the factory defaults.

autostart.label: Start NetRuleRouter tray automatically at sign-in
autostart.description: Adds the tray icon to the programs your system starts when you sign in.

state.overridden: The sign-in entry starts another program file — toggle to repair.

show-welcome.label: Show welcome wizard again...
show-welcome.description: Re-runs the first-launch flow: service install prompt (if not yet installed) and then the preset wizard. Useful when you want to import a different starter rule set.

autoload.title: Auto-load rules on startup
autoload.label: Load rules from the last-used files automatically at startup
autoload.description: When off, NetRuleRouter shows whatever the service already has and does not re-read the files on launch. The remembered file paths are kept.

merge-conflict.title: Merging file and app rules
merge-conflict.description: When you merge a linked rules file with the rules the app is already enforcing, this decides who wins for a rule that exists on both sides but differs. "Ask me" keeps both and lets you pick per rule; "File wins" / "Service wins" resolve automatically.

forget-binding.label: Forget file binding
forget-binding.description: Clears the remembered rules file paths. The next launch loads nothing from disk — you see exactly what the service has.

import-only-active.title: Importing presets
import-only-active.label: Import only active rules
import-only-active.description: When on, rules that are turned off in the imported preset (for example application rules, which can't route yet) are skipped instead of added as disabled rows. Turn off to import everything.

auto-check.label: Check for a new version automatically
auto-check.description: The app asks the project's release page on GitHub whether a newer version is out and shows a notice if it is. Nothing is downloaded or installed, and routing is not touched. The count starts at the first start and restarts after every check, including one from the Help menu. Turned off, the app sends no such request. Takes effect at the next start.

compat-banner-mode.label: Compatibility banner
compat-banner-mode.description: Controls when the GUI shows the version-mismatch banner. "Automatic" only warns on an incompatible protocol.

traffic.title: Traffic statistics
traffic.description: How much traffic goes through the additional (VPN) adapter versus directly over the primary — received and sent per adapter.
traffic.period-today-note: All traffic accounted by the service today, with or without the additional adapter
traffic.period-session-note: Counted while the additional adapter session is active
traffic.session-none: The additional adapter has not come up yet — no session so far
traffic.no-data: No data yet — counting starts once traffic flows.
traffic.service-stopped: Statistics are not being collected while the service is stopped.
traffic.tunnel-overlap-note: While a VPN session is active, the primary row excludes traffic that transited into the tunnel.
traffic.period-all-time-note: Everything counted since the service was installed, split the same way

history-merge.question: "{old}" stopped appearing and "{new}" took its place. Is this the same connection, so its history should continue as one?
history-merge.hint: Answered once. If they are different connections, their histories stay apart and you will not be asked again.

storage.title: Storage usage
storage.description: On-disk footprint of the service state, cache, and log stores.

service-stability.title: Service stability
service-stability.help: These options only affect the control channel (IPC). Network policy enforcement runs independently.
service-stability.reset-tooltip: Reset to factory defaults (recoverable, 20 restarts, 100 ms, 5 s)

recoverable.label: Recoverable (recommended)
recoverable.help: If the GUI ↔ service control channel fails, the supervisor restarts it automatically. Policy enforcement keeps running. After all retry attempts are exhausted, the GUI marks the channel as unavailable but the service continues operating.

critical.label: Critical (fail-fast)
critical.help: Any control-channel failure puts the service into recovery mode. Policy enforcement halts until the operator restarts the service. Use for strict compliance scenarios.

ipc.cap-below-base: Max backoff must be greater than or equal to initial backoff.

verbose.label: Verbose service logging
verbose.tooltip: Adds debug events to the service log. Switches itself off when the chosen time runs out, even across a service restart; the "until the service restarts" choice ends at the next restart. Applies immediately.
verbose.help: Useful for diagnosing rare problems. The log grows substantially while it is on, which is why it switches itself off.

conn-trace.heading: Connection trace (diagnostic)
conn-trace.intro: Records outgoing connections of all apps and the interface each left through (direct vs the additional adapter). Sees the real socket, so it works even when the browser uses DoH. Observation itself is always on — these two controls decide where it is shown and whether it is written down.
conn-trace.intro-no-log: Shows outgoing connections of all apps and the interface each left through (direct vs the additional adapter). Sees the real socket, so it works even when the browser uses DoH. Observation itself is always on — this switch decides whether it is shown. On this platform the trace is never written to disk.

ndjson.label: Write connection trace to service log
ndjson.tooltip: Each observed connection is written to the service log: process, remote IP:port and egress interface (primary or additional adapter). Switches itself off when the chosen time runs out, even across a service restart; the "until the service restarts" choice ends at the next restart. Applies immediately.
ndjson.forced-help: Forced on by the service through {source}. Remove it, then restart the service to control this here again.

gui.label: Show connection trace in Diagnostics
gui.tooltip: Lets the connection-trace panel in Diagnostics show what was observed. Takes effect immediately, no service restart. Switching it off hides the panel's contents only — it does not stop observation, which app routing and rule suggestions rely on.

conn-trace.help: Privacy-sensitive: the trace carries per-connection process names and remote addresses. Writing it to disk is why it switches itself off; leave it off in normal operation.
conn-trace.help-no-log: Privacy-sensitive: the trace carries per-connection process names and remote addresses. It is kept in memory only and is gone when the service restarts.

rule-scope.heading: When routing rules are enforced

service-driven.label: Keep enforcing while the service runs (even when the app is closed)
service-driven.tooltip: On (default): the service enforces your rules continuously — from boot, even with no window or tray icon open — until the service is stopped. Best for always-on or managed/business setups. Off: rules apply only while the app or tray is running; fully exiting the app removes every added route and returns the network to normal.

rule-scope.help: Affects the whole machine and needs administrator approval. On = always-on (managed/business deployments). Off = active only while you keep the app open. Stopping the service always clears the routes.

routing-stop.heading: When routing is paused or the service stops

persist.label: Keep rule routes on the additional adapter after pause/stop (route persistence, not leak protection)
persist.tooltip: Default (off): full teardown — every route is removed and ALL traffic returns to your main connection; matched sites stop using the additional adapter. Turn ON to keep the matched routes on the additional adapter — useful for a work/corporate additional adapter, so you keep reaching corporate resources while general routing is paused; for a general-purpose additional adapter leave it off so everything returns to your main connection. NetRuleRouter's own extra routes are still removed either way. Leak-protection blocks are removed on pause and on a normal stop, so a paused or stopped service does not keep you locked out.

routing-stop.help: Applies to both “safe disable”/pause and stopping the service. Affects the whole machine and needs administrator approval. Note: simply closing the app keeps routing active because the background service keeps running — use Stop service (or Disable) to turn routing off.

cache-refresh.heading: Address cache refresh
cache-refresh.label: Re-resolve routed sites every
cache-refresh.help: How often a routed site's IP addresses are refreshed (1 min – 24 h). Site IPs rarely change, so a longer interval means less network activity; the last known address is always kept and used for routing and leak-protection until a fresh one is obtained, so lengthening this never weakens blocking.

show-audit-tab.label: Show security audit tab
show-audit-tab.help: The security audit trail is always recorded, regardless of this setting. This only shows or hides the audit viewing tab in the Logs view.

conn-history.title: Connection history
conn-history.help: Which of your programs connected where, and over which route, kept on this computer for the days you choose. Only you can read your history; it is never part of the diagnostic archive.
conn-history.retention-a11y: Days the connection history is kept
conn-history.clear-confirm: Erase your whole connection history? This cannot be undone.
conn-history.cleared: Your connection history was erased (%1 entries).
conn-history.clear-failed: Could not erase the connection history:
conn-history.save-failed: Could not save the connection history choice:

mutes.heading: Active mutes
mutes.load-failed: Could not load the mute list:

add.heading: Add a mute
add.description: The notification's quick-mute options only offer a few fixed lengths. Use this form for a duration of your own, or to mute indefinitely.
add.host-placeholder: Hostname, exactly as shown in the notification
add.app-placeholder: Application (process) name, exactly as shown in the notification

theme.system-undetected: The system theme could not be determined — using the light theme.

language.diagnostics-summary: %1 locale file(s) reported problems. The affected keys fall back to English; everything else in the file is used.

hidden.heading: Hidden notifications
hidden.description: Choose for how long each kind of notification stays hidden. The "Don't show…" button on a notification sets the same thing.

notifications.site-not-opening: A site does not open (told even while the tray is closed)

vpn-onboarding.gateway-allowed-status: The VPN server {address} can now be reached while leak protection is on.
vpn-onboarding.gateway-save-failed: Could not save the change to the allowed VPN servers, so nothing changed. Try again.
vpn-onboarding.title: Your VPN client
vpn-onboarding.heading: Do you use a VPN?
vpn-onboarding.intro: Point NetRuleRouter at it so it keeps working when leak protection is on. We look at your running programs and installed apps — nothing is sent anywhere.
vpn-onboarding.multi-hint: Tick every program that's part of your VPN — for example a client together with its background service or command-line helper. All of them will keep working over your main link.
vpn-onboarding.empty: No VPN apps found. If you use one, pick it manually below.
vpn-onboarding.not-scanned-yet: Run a scan to look for VPN apps.
vpn-onboarding.scan-failed: Could not scan for VPN apps. You can pick your VPN manually below.
vpn-onboarding.not-read: Your VPN programs could not be read, so they cannot be changed now.
vpn-onboarding.manual-pick: My VPN isn't listed / pick it manually
vpn-onboarding.confirmed-status: NetRuleRouter will keep {name} working over your main link while leak protection is on.
vpn-onboarding.cleared-status: No program is kept working over your main link any more.
vpn-onboarding.skipped-status: No VPN set up. You can set one up later from Settings -> Routing.
vpn-onboarding.service-write-failed: Could not save to the routing service — will retry on next apply.
vpn-onboarding.kernel-tunnel-assign: Kernel tunnel {name} — assign adapter {interface} as the additional link
vpn-onboarding.kernel-tunnel-why: The system itself runs this tunnel, so no program rule can carry it — it is routed by its adapter.

app-groups.title: Application and device routes
app-groups.subtitle: detected on this computer
app-groups.entry-note: Assign a route to the virtual machines, emulators and peer-to-peer apps found on this computer.
app-groups.empty: Nothing detected on this computer. You can add a program as an ordinary application rule.
app-groups.vm-note: Virtual machine traffic follows the route assigned to its program. The default is the main route. A machine's local networks (host-to-guest access) always keep working, whichever route you pick.
app-groups.p2p-note: These programs are not blocked unless leak protection is on. The assigned route applies to their bulk connections; their peers are not added to zone rules.
app-groups.kernel-nat-note: Traffic of WSL, Hyper-V, Docker, libvirt and other virtual machines does not belong to any program on this computer, so it cannot be given a route of its own. When it goes out through this computer, it follows the routes your rules set, as this computer's own traffic does; a machine bridged straight onto your network goes past them. Flexible routing for these environments is planned for the future.
app-groups.footer-note: Can't find your program? Add it as an ordinary application rule, or tell us through any channel — the dictionary keeps growing.
app-groups.legend-running: running — the process is active right now
app-groups.legend-installed: installed — found in the program list
app-groups.legend-feature: system component — detected via an OS service

status.detail-active: Rules apply on this user session.
status.detail-limited: Some rules are not being applied right now. The notices say why.
status.detail-paused: Rules are disabled for the time chosen; they come back on their own when it is up, or when you turn them back on.
status.detail-no-tray: Run the tray icon to apply rules on this session.
status.detail-no-rules: Add rules in the Rules section, then click Save and review.
status.detail-disconnected: Showing preview data. Install and start the NetRuleRouter service to apply rules.

status-text.preview-mode: First-run setup is not finished: your rules are not applied yet.
status-text.checking-status: Checking whether the service is reachable and whether your rules are being applied.
status-text.no-active-policy: Your rules are not being applied right now.
status-text.service-unavailable: The background service is not reachable: rules cannot be applied or changed until it is back.

setup-state.allowed: Action is available in the current setup state.
setup-state.soft-guided: Available; finishing the first-run setup first is recommended.
setup-state.blocked-until-wizard-completion: Available once the first-run setup is finished.

tray.preview-only-note: This action is not available yet.

host-start.title: NetRuleRouter cannot start
host-start.missing-library: The installation is incomplete: reinstall the program.
host-start.missing-named-library: The installation is incomplete: the library {library} is missing. Reinstall the program or install the library with your package manager.
host-start.outdated-library: The library {library} on this system is too old: the program needs version {version}. Update it with your package manager, or use the terminal interface: run nrr-tui.

offline-backlog.title: Changes made while the service was stopped
offline-backlog.body: The service is running again. These changes were made while it was stopped and are not in effect yet.
offline-backlog.preview-description: Show what would change in the service; nothing is applied.
offline-backlog.discard-hint: Discarding only stops the offer — the rules stay in the table and nothing on screen is lost.
offline-backlog.later-description: Keep the changes pending and ask again next time the service connects.

full-reset.title: Full reset
full-reset.body: This resets ALL application settings to defaults, deletes the rules the service keeps for you (back to a post-install state), wipes saved comments and logs, and stops the background service. Your own rules files on disk are left untouched, and the background service is NOT uninstalled. This cannot be undone.
full-reset.ack: I understand this erases all settings and applied rules
full-reset.other-users: Other users of this computer have rules here too ({count}). What should be cleared?
full-reset.scope-everyone: Every user on this computer (asks for administrator approval)

full-reset-done.title: Full reset complete
full-reset-done.body: Full reset is done. To apply it the program and the tray must be fully closed. Close them now?
full-reset-done.service-warn: Note: some service-side data could not be cleared (administrator approval may be required, or a temporary error occurred). Re-run the reset.

build-mismatch.title: Another build is already running
build-mismatch.body: NetRuleRouter is already open and it is a different build: {running}. The one you just started is {ours}. Close the open NetRuleRouter window (quit it from the tray icon too), then start the application again.

nothing-to-apply.title: Nothing to apply
nothing-to-apply.body: There are no changes to apply — the current rules already match what is active.

reset-baseline-noop.title: Already on baseline
reset-baseline-noop.body: You have no custom rules — the baseline rules are already in effect.

rule.enabled-off: Rule is disabled (kept in the file, not applied)
rule.duplicate-body: A rule with the same type, value, and target route already exists ({id}). Open the existing rule to change it, or cancel to keep editing the new one.
rule.coverage-with-subdomains: Covers {host} and every subdomain of it.
rule.coverage-exact-only: Covers {host} only. Type *.{host} to include its subdomains.
rule.coverage-any-zone: Covers {host} in every zone ({host}.com, {host}.net and so on) with all subdomains. A rule naming the zone wins over it.

path.choose-folder-title: Choose the folder with the programs
path.count-more: Programs covered now: the first {count}. The folder holds more than one rule covers.
path.missing: Nothing is there yet: the rule takes effect once the program or folder appears.
path.unsupported: This system does not apply rules by path yet.
path.anyone-can-write: Anyone can put a program here, so the rule may cover programs you did not install. A program here is never exempt from leak protection.

rule.verify-hint: Works through the route it is written for. If the site or address does not open there but does on the other route, NetRuleRouter offers to move the rule.
rule.verify-any-zone: A site in every zone is not checked: the check needs one host.
rule.verify-deny: A denied rule is not checked: its traffic goes through no connection.
rule.verify-ipv6: An IPv6 address is not checked: the check goes out over IPv4 only, so this stays an ordinary route rule.

bulk.label: One rule per line, as in a rules file: !value denies, ?value checks where it works, # value is kept switched off, and a line such as --- Windows gives the lines below it their type. Otherwise the type is read from the value.
bulk.summary: To add: {add}. To move: {move}. Stay in the field: {keep}. Already in your rules: {drop}.
bulk.bound-lines: Only the first {max} lines are read; the other {count} stay in the field for the next round.
bulk.bound-size: The text is longer than one round reads: the first {lines} lines are read, the other {count} stay in the field.

load-list.title: Load rule list
load-list.intro: Pick one or two preset .txt files — one per route. Leaving a slot empty keeps that route's current rules untouched.
load-list.same-file-conflict: The same file cannot be selected for both the primary and the additional route at the same time.
load-list.mode-replace: Replace current rules with the imported set
load-list.mode-replace-description: Existing rules for the imported route(s) are cleared first.
load-list.mode-merge: Merge — add new rules, skip duplicates
load-list.mode-merge-description: Keeps current rules (with your manual edits and comments). Imported rules with the same type, value and route are skipped.

license.note: Third-party notices and full texts are wired as a separate step.

import-rule-file-not-found.title: Rules file not found
import-rule-file-not-found.message: The rules file from the imported configuration was not found at its stored path. Choose how to proceed.

file-too-large.title: File too large
file-too-large.description: The preset file exceeds the 1 MB size limit. Reduce the number of rules or split across multiple files.

encoding-error.title: Encoding error
encoding-error.description: The file is not valid UTF-8. Open it in a text editor and re-save with UTF-8 encoding.

too-many-rules.title: Too many rules
too-many-rules.description: The preset file contains more than 9,999 rules, which exceeds the active rule limit. Remove some rules and try again.

match-value-too-long.title: Match value too long
match-value-too-long.description: One or more match values in this file exceed the 260-character limit. Shorten them and try again.

control-character.title: Unsupported character
control-character.description: A value, comment or header line in this file contains a control character. Remove it in a text editor and try again.

warning.extended-section-skipped: Contains extended sections — their rules are not applied in this version

provenance.gui-rules-edit: Source: rules edited in this app.

review-diff.title: Review changes

reset-summary.one: Discard {count} custom rule and restore the baseline rules.
reset-summary.other: Discard {count} custom rules and restore the baseline rules.

review-diff.reset-files: Your linked rules files will be rewritten with the baseline rules: {files}.
review-diff.approve-description: Proceed to the activation confirmation step
review-diff.apply-description: Apply the reviewed rule set and start the activation
review-diff.cancel-description: Cancel the activation and keep the previous rule set
review-diff.close-description: Close the preview without applying anything
review-diff.apply-from-preview-description: Close the preview and open the activation flow for these parked changes
review-diff.no-elevation-warning: NetRuleRouter is not running as administrator. When you apply, the system will ask for administrator approval.
review-diff.session-elevation-active: You granted administrator approval for this session. Changes apply without another prompt. This temporary approval ends when you close NetRuleRouter.
review-diff.duplicates-hint: Each of these is enabled on both routes, so which one carries the traffic is decided by evaluation order rather than by you. Pick the route that should keep it — the other copy stays in your list, switched off.
review-diff.summary-rules-unchanged: The rule list does not change; routing is rebuilt from it.

reload-from-service.title: Load active rules from the service?
reload-from-service.body: You have unsaved changes to the rules. Loading the active rules from the service will discard them. Continue?

rules-file-edited.title: A rules file was edited outside the app
rules-file-edited.body: Your rules changed elsewhere, and this file was edited by hand since the app last saved it, so it was left as it is. Take the file to compare it with the rules in force and apply what you keep, or replace the file with the rules in force.

unroutable-secondary.title: This adapter cannot carry traffic out
unroutable-secondary.body-assign: You are about to assign it as your additional route.
unroutable-secondary.body-assign-primary: You are about to make it your main connection.
unroutable-secondary.body-kill-switch: It is currently assigned as your additional route.
unroutable-secondary.reason-virtual-host-only: It looks like a host-only virtual adapter (VirtualBox, VMware or Hyper-V internal) and it has no gateway, so it has no way out to the network.
unroutable-secondary.reason-no-forwarding-path: It has no gateway and no route out, so there is nowhere for it to send traffic.
unroutable-secondary.effect-routing: Rules that point at the additional route will not be routed through it.
unroutable-secondary.effect-routing-primary: The service will not route through it: traffic your rules do not route keeps going the way the system sends it. Choose the connection that reaches the internet as main.
unroutable-secondary.effect-kill-switch-on: Leak protection is on, so those destinations are BLOCKED instead: the sites behind those rules stop loading.
unroutable-secondary.effect-kill-switch-off: Leak protection is off right now, so nothing is blocked. If you turn it on later, those destinations will be blocked.
unroutable-secondary.effect-kill-switch-arming: Once leak protection is on, those destinations are BLOCKED instead: the sites behind those rules stop loading.

leak-holds-now.title: The additional connection is not available
leak-holds-now.body: With leak protection set to Everything, traffic is held right away: the internet stops until the additional connection returns.
leak-holds-now.effect: Your local network and what your rules send over the main connection keep working.
leak-holds-now.role-title: Leak protection will hold all traffic
leak-holds-now.role-body: Leak protection is set to Everything. Without an available additional connection, traffic is held right away: the internet stops until an available adapter is the additional connection again.

factory-preset-save.title: This file belongs to the app's own rule sets
factory-preset-save.body: The rules file you are saving to is one of the sets that come with the app, and the next update replaces that folder — anything saved there would be lost. Save into a folder of your own instead, or save here anyway if that is what you want.

overwrite-set.title: This set already has saved rules
overwrite-set.body: The folder you chose already has a primary or additional-route rules file in it. Saving here replaces them.

empty-service-rules.title: The service has no active rules

body.one: The background service is currently enforcing 0 rules. Loading its state will remove the {count} rule shown here. Your rules files on disk are not touched. Continue?
body.other: The background service is currently enforcing 0 rules. Loading its state will remove all {count} rules shown here. Your rules files on disk are not touched. Continue?

safe-rollback.title: Roll back to the previous configuration?
safe-rollback.body-loading: Looking for the previous version of your rules…
safe-rollback.body-ready: Your current rules will be replaced by the ones you applied on {time} ({count} rules), and routing will follow them right away.
safe-rollback.body-none: There is nothing to roll back to: no earlier version of your rules has been applied.

service-not-running.title: Service not running
service-not-running.body: The NetRuleRouter service is not running. Rule changes cannot be applied to the network until it is. You can start the service now, save your rules to a file, park the changes for later, or cancel.
service-not-running.save-to-file-description: Write the current rules to your rules files. This works with the service stopped.
service-not-running.stale-pending-warning: There is already a parked changeset (+{added} / -{removed} / ~{modified}). Choosing "Work without service" will replace it.
service-not-running.start-service-description: Start the background service (requires administrator privileges).
service-not-running.install-service-description: Install the background service (requires administrator privileges) and start it.
service-not-running.work-without-description: Park the changes locally; they will not be applied to the network until the service is running.
service-not-running.cancel-description: Dismiss the dialog without applying or parking the changes.

export-options.title: Export options
export-options.body: Customize what to include in the preset file.
export-options.include-comments-description: When on, each rule's ` # comment` suffix is written to the file. Turn off to share rules without your personal notes.
export-options.no-comments-hint: Comments will be stripped from the exported file. Existing comments in the app are not affected.

drift.title: Rules drift detected
drift.body: The rules stored in your file, shown in the app, and applied by the service no longer agree. Pick how to resolve.
drift.load-from-file-description: Load the saved file(s) into the app table, replacing local edits. Apply when ready.
drift.accept-service-description: Discard local edits and roll back the app to what the service holds.
drift.apply-gui-description: Open the review flow and push the current app state to the service.
drift.show-diff-description: Open a read-only diff of the current app rules against the service.
drift.clear-all-description: Remove all rules from the app and the service. This cannot be undone.
drift.not-now-description: Dismiss the dialog. The banner stays until the drift is resolved.
drift.merge-description: Your linked rules file and the service's active rules have diverged. Merge combines both instead of choosing one side.

merge.duplicates-hint: Each of these was enabled on both routes, so the merge kept the main route's copy and switched the other one off. Pick a different route if that is not what you meant — the other copy stays in your list, switched off.
merge.title: Merge file and app rules
merge.edits-title: Your edits and the rules now in force
merge.edits-body: Your rules were changed elsewhere while you were editing them. Your edits go on top of the rules now in force: a rule you added, changed or deleted is added, changed or deleted there too, and rules changed elsewhere stay. Where both sides changed the same rule you pick the version that stays.
merge.edits-loading: Comparing your edits with the rules in force…

auto-rules-mode.title: Turn on “Apply automatically”?
auto-rules-mode.body: From now on NetRuleRouter will add suggested addresses to your rules files by itself, without asking. You can undo this anytime by switching back to “Suggest only”.

first-launch-install.title: Welcome to NetRuleRouter
first-launch-install.body-1: NetRuleRouter applies routing rules from a background system service so they persist across reboots and user sessions.
first-launch-install.body-2: Installing the service requires Administrator approval (UAC). After install, the service starts automatically.
first-launch-install.body-3: You can skip this step and use NetRuleRouter in read-only preview mode, but routing rules will not apply.

reset-script.title: Emergency network reset script

eula.title: License agreement
eula.heading: Please read and accept the agreement to continue
eula.subheading: Installing, running, or using NetRuleRouter means you accept the terms below.

uac-required.title: Administrator approval required

admin-required.title: Administrator rights required
admin-required.body: Applying rules changes Windows routing filters, which requires administrator rights. Close NetRuleRouter and start it again as administrator (right-click → "Run as administrator"), then apply the changes. Viewing rules and the service status works without administrator rights.

first-run-wizard.title: Welcome to NetRuleRouter
first-run-wizard.description: Choose how to populate your initial rule set. You can change it later from the Rules toolbar or in Settings → Presets and settings.
first-run-wizard.option-country-preset-description: Detected from your OS locale. Imports the bundled pack for your region.
first-run-wizard.location-abroad: I am {where} and need access to its services
first-run-wizard.option-country-preset-abroad-description: Everything stays on your local provider; only that country's services take the additional route.

first-run-wizard.option-builtin-demo-description: A tiny showcase set covering each rule kind. Replace with your own later.
first-run-wizard.option-open-file-description: Choose one or two preset .txt files — one for each route. Leave a route empty to start it blank.
first-run-wizard.option-start-empty-description: No rules. Add or import them whenever you want.
first-run-wizard.protection-description: Recommended for everyone. Each of these can be changed later in Settings.
first-run-wizard.protection-doh-lockdown: Keep browsers from resolving routed sites past NetRuleRouter
first-run-wizard.protection-fake-ip: Route sites by name, so an address shared with another site is not dragged along (uses a virtual network adapter; on Windows this loads its Wintun driver)
first-run-wizard.protection-diagnostic-logs: Write detailed diagnostic logs (only needed to report a problem)
first-run-wizard.protection-mute-block-notices: Do not show notifications about blocked traffic (rule suggestions still arrive)
first-run-wizard.site-notice-note: Even with the tray closed, NetRuleRouter tells you when a site you open does not open over the main connection. You can turn this off in Settings, Notifications.
first-run-wizard.primary-adapter-description: The connection everything travels by default. Until you name it, your rules are not applied.
first-run-wizard.primary-adapter-assigned: Main connection: {name}. You can change it later in Interfaces and routes.

preset-review.title: Review preset import
preset-review.intro: The file contains sections that need a decision before import.
preset-review.duplicates-hint: These sections appear more than once in the file. Pick how to combine them.
preset-review.unknowns-hint: We didn't recognise these sections. Tell us what they are, or keep them as-is for export.

save-before-close.title: Save rule changes?
save-before-close.intro: Active rules differ from the files you imported. Without saving, those edits will be rolled back.

save-before-close.row-no-path: (no file yet — choose with Save As...)

confirm-activate.body-low: These changes look safe. Apply them now?
confirm-activate.body-medium: These changes affect routing scope. Apply them now?
confirm-activate.body-high: These changes have a high impact on routing. Apply them now?
confirm-activate.body-critical: These changes could lock you out of the network. Read the risk signals carefully before confirming.

review-expired.title: Review session expired
review-expired.body: Your confirmation token expired before the change was applied. Compare the changes again to refresh the review.
review-expired.compare-again-description: Re-run the review against the current rule set
review-expired.cancel-description: Dismiss the dialog without retrying the review

safe-disable.title: Turn off rules for a while
safe-disable.body: Your routing and leak protection stop for the time you choose: the routes and filters NetRuleRouter keeps for you are removed, and they come back on their own when it is up. Other users of this computer keep theirs. The service stays running; you can turn the rules back on earlier. This action is audited.
safe-disable.reason-required: Please describe the reason — it is recorded in the audit trail.
safe-disable.confirm-description: Temporarily disable enforcement with the provided reason
safe-disable.cancel-description: Dismiss the dialog and leave enforcement active
safe-disable.unavailable: Safe disable requires the NetRuleRouter service to be running. Start the service and try again.

term.until-restart: After the computer or the service restarts
term.until-resumed: When I turn them back on

network-recovery.title: Restore network?
network-recovery.body: The packet filters, DNS redirect and routes the service applied will be removed, leak protection included. Connections open right now may drop, and until the service applies its rules again, routing is off and sites meant for the additional adapter can go over the main connection. Administrator rights are required.
network-recovery.overrides: Rules you confirmed despite the protection of system programs are revoked.
network-recovery.body-stop: The service will be stopped, and ended if it does not stop in half a minute; then the packet filters, DNS redirect and routes it applied are removed, leak protection included. Connections open right now may drop, and until the service is started again, routing is off and sites meant for the additional adapter can go over the main connection. Administrator rights are required.

service-update.title: Update the background service?
service-update.body: The service will be registered from this folder and restarted. Routing pauses for a moment; your rules, settings and history are kept. Administrator rights are required.

rules-overlap.title: Remove rules already covered
rules-overlap.body: These rules name a host that one of your wildcard rules already covers. Removing them changes nothing about where your traffic goes — it only shortens the list.
rules-overlap.deliberate-body: These name a host under a wildcard but deny it, or apply only to one program. That is what an exception looks like, so nothing here is removed for you. Rules that send a host over the other route are listed under Rules → Overlaps.
rules-overlap.keep-tooltip: Leave this rule alone and stop offering it here.
rules-overlap.empty: Nothing is covered twice right now.

rules.application-routing-note-linux: Routes everything this program connects to through the additional connection. NetRuleRouter learns the program's destinations by watching its connections, so routing fills in as it connects. Enter the process name, e.g. browser.

import-only-active.label: Import only active rules
import-only-active.tooltip: When loading a preset, skip rules that are turned off in it (for example application rules, which can't route yet). Default comes from Settings → General; changing it here applies to imports this session only.

hint.zone: A zone — letters, digits, hyphens, parts separated by dots; an optional leading dot is allowed. Matches all hosts in the zone. Examples: .ru, ru, com, intra, corp.internal.
hint.domain: FQDN (example.com), wildcard suffix (*.example.com) or the site in every zone (example.*). Matches the domain itself and all subdomains. Examples: example.com, *.example.com, mail.example.com, example.*.
hint.exact-ip: Exact IPv4 or IPv6 address. For IPv4 each octet is 0–255 and the first is ≥ 1. Examples: 192.0.2.1, 203.0.113.7, 2001:db8::7.
hint.application-windows: Process filename — .exe, .ps1, .bat or any executable script. Exact (browser.exe) or glob (*vpn*.exe).
hint.application-macos: Process filename or app bundle id.
hint.subnet: A network in CIDR form: an address, a slash and the prefix length. Matches every address in the network; an address with host bits set is saved as its network. Examples: 10.0.0.0/8, 198.51.100.0/24, 2001:db8::/32.
hint.ip-range: Two addresses of the same family joined by a dash, the first not greater than the last. Matches every address from the first to the last inclusive. Examples: 192.0.2.10-192.0.2.40, 2001:db8::1-2001:db8::ff.
